question: The Erasmus+ Key Action 2 Cooperation Partnerships in higher education (HE) have been instrumental in enabling bottom-up initiatives led by higher education institutions to internationalise HE and deepen cooperation between institutions and stakeholders. From 2023 to 2025, the budget allocated to this funding line has been cut from EUR 121 million to EUR 73 million.

Furthermore, it is the lowest budget allocation since 2019, not even considering the cost increase. In the meantime, the number of applications has substantially increased, demonstrating the need for this funding model. 1.
Why has the decision been made to drastically decrease the funding allocated to this budget line, while the HE community’s uptake of this cooperation opportunity has been significant?
Where is the Key Action 2 Partnership Cooperation funding being redirected, considering the overall Erasmus+ budget has been increasing?

Are political priorities informing this strategic budgetary decision (if so, which ones), and have stakeholder organisations, Member States and Members of the European Parliament been consulted on this question?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2025) The 2021-2027 Erasmus+ regulation1 foresees a budget distribution across its sectors and between management modes. No fixed budget is allocated to learning mobility and cooperation projects within sectors. Instead, the Regulation envisions expanding learning mobility opportunities to extend its reach and satisfy the demand.

On this basis, the Commission has prioritised support for learning mobility2, as endorsed by the Programme Committee. The European Parliament3 further called to keep Erasmus+ close to the people and ensure it remains a ‘citizens’ programme’ offering quality education and mobility opportunities for young people and learners of all ages. This approach was supported in recent consultations4.

Between 2021 and 2024, the average success rate of Key Action 2 cooperation partnerships in higher education was 31% (total grant amount: EUR 446 million), in line with the period 2017-2020 (32%, EUR 416 million granted). This rate is higher compared to the success rate of cooperation partnerships across sectors (21%). Also, national agencies can reallocate budgets with a specific margin based on assessed needs.

Transnational cooperation remains key to Erasmus+, supporting modernisation, skills development, and the green and digital transitions. Together with other forms of partnerships, Cooperation Partnerships contribute to these objectives, driving reforms and contributing to the Union of Skills5.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/817 of 20 May 2021. 2 During the Covid-19 pandemic allocations for cooperation was temporarily increased due to restrictions on

mobility. 3 Resolution of 16 January 2024 on the implementation of the 2021-2027 Erasmus+ programme. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/13454-Erasmus+-2021-27-interimevaluation-Erasmus+-2014-20-final-evaluation_en. 5 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-competitiveness/union-skills_en.
